about: The location filter's meaning, as data. Prose is in
docs/claude/location-filter-semantics.md; this file is what the tests
actually run, because the same rule is transcribed FOUR times and nothing
but a shared table can keep them in step:
combo  scifor.locations         — a dict predicate over for_each combos
row    scistackplot.reduce      — a vectorised pandas mask
row    scistackplot.codegen     — the same mask, EMITTED as plain pandas
tree   locationSelection.ts     — checkbox coverage in the GUI
scistackplot cannot import scifor (pandas/numpy/scistacklog only), so the
copies are real. Adding a case here fails every implementation that has
not adopted it, which is the point: a suite that hand-copied the table
would silently keep passing.
applies_to: which implementations a case is meaningful for.
'combo' — scifor. A combo may be COARSER than a location (a run
iterating subject only), which rows never are.
'row'   — the pandas sides. `location` becomes a one-row DataFrame, so a
key absent from `location` is an absent COLUMN, and a null is
NaN. JSON types are deliberate: 1.0 is a float column, 1 an
int one, "01" a string one.
'tree'  — the GUI's coverage walk. `location` becomes a single chain of
nodes, one per key, and the case asks what the LEAF's checkbox
shows: 'full' for in, 'none' for out. Null cases are absent
here on purpose — a location tree has no null steps, because a
key a record was not saved at simply contributes no node.

cases.name: empty-pair-is-inert
cases.why: Clicking into a picker is not a statement. 'Everything selected' and 'never opened' must store the same thing.

cases.name: covered-by-prefix
cases.why: The ordinary case.

cases.name: uncovered-by-prefix
cases.why: A non-empty include excludes everything it does not cover.

cases.name: level-rule-drops-it
cases.why: The left pane's standing rule.

cases.name: the-rule-survives-new-data
cases.why: Subject 09 did not exist when the rule was written. This is why exclude_levels is a rule and not exploded prefixes: exploding would freeze today's subjects and drop tomorrow's entirely.

cases.name: exclusion-beats-coverage
cases.why: The rule is applied AFTER coverage and always wins; it is never merged into it.

cases.name: ragged-prefix-skipping-a-key
cases.why: A prefix names its keys, so it can skip one — a cross-cutting selection of subject+trial is not subject+session.

cases.name: ragged-prefix-excludes-siblings
cases.why: Every named key must match.

cases.name: values-compare-as-text
cases.why: Every selection crosses JSON, so an int 3 and a string "3" are one value.

cases.name: absent-key-is-not-a-match
cases.why: A cross-cutting record saved at subject+speed has no timepoint step, so a timepoint rule does not touch it. Reading positionally would match the value against the wrong key and select nothing, in silence.

cases.name: every-level-excluded-selects-nothing
cases.why: Legal, and reported rather than corrected.

cases.name: ancestor-combo-is-kept
cases.why: A run iterating subject only, against a selection naming trial: some of what this combo covers was selected, and dropping it would silently run nothing. No row counterpart — a row always carries every key it was saved at.

cases.name: ancestor-rule-does-not-weaken-a-mismatch
cases.why: Ignoring keys the combo LACKS must not start ignoring keys it HAS.

cases.name: empty-prefix-inside-include-means-everything
cases.why: A prefix constraining no keys constrains nothing. The two sides reach this by different routes (a vacuous all() vs the 'names no known column' path), so it is pinned rather than assumed.

cases.name: overlapping-prefixes-are-idempotent
cases.why: include is a union. A prefix covered by another one changes nothing — the picker normalises to a minimal covering set, but a hand-written spec need not.

cases.name: integral-float-matches-its-integer-spelling
cases.why: A schema key that round-tripped through DuckDB as a float gives the pandas side "1.0" while the picker (whose tree comes from scidb) gives "1". Comparing raw text would silently select nothing across that seam, so a value is matched against the numeric spellings of itself.

cases.name: zero-padding-is-identity-not-a-number
cases.why: Guards case 16 from eating the padding rule: "01" and "1" can be two distinct trials, and which spelling is identity is scidb's decision (schema-key-types.md), never a comparison shortcut here.

cases.name: a-non-integral-float-keeps-its-own-spelling
cases.why: Case 16 normalises only the .0 tail; 1.5 must still match itself.

cases.name: a-null-key-matches-no-real-value
cases.why: NULL at a key is not a level. The two sides spell it differently (NaN vs None) and must agree on the outcome anyway.

cases.name: a-null-key-is-not-excluded-by-a-level-rule
cases.why: The contrast to case 19: a null is not the excluded level either, so the row survives. Getting this wrong drops every cross-cutting record the moment any rule exists.

cases.name: values-are-case-sensitive
cases.why: Folding case would merge two levels a dataset may genuinely distinguish.

cases.name: separator-lookalikes-are-matched-literally
cases.why: ' / ' is how a selection is DISPLAYED (describeSelection); it is not a delimiter in the stored form, and a level containing it must not be parsed as two steps.

cases.name: a-rule-naming-an-absent-key-drops-nothing
cases.why: The row-side twin of case 10: a table that never carried `trial` (a subject-level variable) must not lose every row to a trial rule.

cases.name: an-include-naming-only-absent-keys-is-inert
cases.why: A subject-level Mass contributes its one value to every trial. Both sides keep the row and SAY SO (a warning naming the unmatched keys), rather than returning an empty figure with no explanation.
